title: Data Interpretation
weightage: High — every GRE Quant section includes a Data Interpretation set of 2–3 linked questions
intro: Data Interpretation is the one place on the GRE where several questions hang off a single figure — a table, a pair of graphs, or a pie chart — so a few minutes spent reading the display carefully pays off across two or three questions. The maths itself is deliberately gentle: percentages, ratios, averages and simple differences. The difficulty is entirely in the reading — which row, which axis, which whole, which units, and whether the question wants an exact value or an estimate. The GRE rewards test-takers who orient to a chart before touching a number: read the title, the axis labels and the footnotes first. This chapter drills the four display types the GRE reuses — tables, bar and line graphs, pie/circle graphs, and multi-source sets — and the estimation habits that let you skip the slow on-screen calculator whenever the answer choices are far apart.

items.name: Average of several bars
items.formula: (sum of the bar heights) / (number of bars)

items.name: Estimation cue
items.formula: if the answer choices are far apart, round and skip the calculator

topics.name: Reading Tables
topics.details: A table is the densest way the GRE presents data, so the first move is orientation: read the title, then the column headers and the row labels, and note the units (dollars? thousands? percent?). Many table questions are answered by locating a single cell — the intersection of the right row and column — but the harder ones ask you to combine cells: a total across a row, a difference between two years, or a percent of a column total. Watch for two classic traps. First, tables often report figures "in thousands" or "in millions", so a cell reading 12 may mean 12,000; multiply consistently or, better, work in the table’s own units and only scale at the end. Second, a "% of total" question demands the correct whole — a column subtotal is not the grand total. Compute the total once, jot it down, and reuse it across the linked questions.

solved.problem: A table of monthly sales (in $ thousands): Jan 40, Feb 55, Mar 65, Apr 50. What were total sales, in dollars, for the first quarter (Jan–Mar)?
solved.solution: Jan + Feb + Mar = 40 + 55 + 65 = 160 (thousand). In dollars that is 160 × 1000 = $160,000.

solved.problem: Same table (Jan 40, Feb 55, Mar 65, Apr 50, in $ thousands). By what percent did sales rise from January to March?
A table shows units sold by two stores: Store X — 120, 140, 160 over three months; Store Y — 80, 100, 120. What was Store X’s average monthly sales?

Quantitative Comparison. From the same table (X: 120, 140, 160; Y: 80, 100, 120), Quantity A: total units sold by Store X over the three months. Quantity B: total units sold by Store Y plus 200. Which is greater?
solved.solution: X total = 420. Y total = 80 + 100 + 120 = 300, plus 200 = 500. 420 < 500, so Quantity B is greater.

unsolved.problem: A table (in $ millions): Product A 8, B 12, C 5, D 15. Total revenue in dollars?
Same table (A 8, B 12, C 5, D 15, $ millions). Product B is what percent of total revenue?
A class table lists marks: 5 students at 60, 3 at 70, 2 at 90. What is the class average?
hints: Weight each mark by its count.

unsolved.problem: A table of costs (in thousands): 2019 → 250, 2020 → 300. Percent increase over the year?
A table shows exports by region: North 45, South 30, East 15, West 10 (in $ thousands). East and West combined are what fraction of the total?

topics.name: Bar & Line Graphs
topics.details: Bar graphs compare separate categories by bar height; line graphs track how one quantity changes across an ordered axis, usually time. Before computing anything, read the vertical scale: note where it starts (a truncated axis that begins at 40 instead of 0 exaggerates differences), the gridline spacing, and the units. For bars, the height is the value and questions turn into differences, ratios or averages of heights. For lines, the slope carries the meaning — a steep upward segment is a fast increase, a flat segment is no change, a downward segment is a decrease — and the steepest segment, not the highest point, marks the greatest rate of change. A grouped or stacked bar chart layers two data series; make sure you are reading the right series (check the legend) and, for a stacked bar, that you subtract to isolate a single segment rather than reading the cumulative top.

solved.problem: A line graph of revenue: Year 1 = $20M, Year 2 = $28M, Year 3 = $35M, Year 4 = $32M. Which one-year interval had the largest increase?
solved.solution: Year-over-year changes: +8, +7, −3. The largest increase is +8, from Year 1 to Year 2.

solved.problem: A bar graph shows visitors (in thousands): Mon 12, Tue 9, Wed 15, Thu 18, Fri 21. What was the average daily number of visitors?
A grouped bar chart shows, for 2022, imports = 60 and exports = 45 (in $ billion). Imports exceeded exports by what percent?
solved.solution: Difference = 60 − 45 = 15 on a base of exports = 45. (15/45) × 100 = 33.3%.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. On a line graph, profit rises from 30 to 45 between Q1 and Q2, then from 45 to 55 between Q2 and Q3. Quantity A: the percent increase in Q1→Q2. Quantity B: the percent increase in Q2→Q3. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Q1→Q2: (15/30)×100 = 50%. Q2→Q3: (10/45)×100 ≈ 22.2%. So Quantity A is greater. (Note the later jump is larger in raw units but smaller in percent because the base grew.)

unsolved.problem: A line graph reads 100, 130, 150, 140 over four years. Which interval shows a decrease?
hints: Compare each year to the previous.

unsolved.problem: Bars (in thousands): 8, 12, 10, 14, 16. Average value?
A grouped bar shows 2021 sales = 50 and 2022 sales = 65 ($ million). Percent increase?
A line rises from 40 to 60, then 60 to 66. Which segment has the greater percent increase?
hints: Compute each relative to its start.

unsolved.problem: A stacked bar for one month shows a total of 90 with the "online" segment topping out at 90 above an "in-store" segment of 55. How large is the online segment?
hints: A stacked bar’s top is the cumulative total.

topics.name: Pie & Circle Graphs
topics.details: A pie (circle) graph shows how a single total is divided into shares, so every slice is a percent of one whole and all slices sum to 100% (or, in angle terms, 360°). Two conversions unlock every pie question. To turn a slice into a real quantity, multiply its percent by the grand total: a 35% slice of $80,000 is 0.35 × 80,000 = $28,000. To move between a slice’s angle and its percent, use percent = (angle/360) × 100 — a 90° slice is a quarter, i.e. 25%. The most common GRE trap is comparing two different pies: a bigger slice of a smaller pie can represent fewer actual units than a smaller slice of a larger pie, because percentages are relative to different totals. Never compare slice sizes across two charts without first converting each to an absolute number using its own total.

solved.problem: A household budget pie: Rent 40%, Food 25%, Transport 15%, Savings 20%. If total monthly income is $3,200, how much goes to Food?
In the same budget, how many degrees does the Rent slice span?
A pie of 1,200 survey respondents shows "Prefer tea" as a 30% slice and "Prefer coffee" as a 45% slice. How many more chose coffee than tea?

Quantitative Comparison. Company X has 5,000 employees; 20% work in Sales. Company Y has 3,000 employees; 40% work in Sales. Quantity A: Sales staff at X. Quantity B: Sales staff at Y. Which is greater?
solved.solution: X: 0.20 × 5000 = 1000. Y: 0.40 × 3000 = 1200. 1000 < 1200, so Quantity B is greater — the smaller percent of the larger company still trails, illustrating why you must convert to absolute numbers.

unsolved.problem: A pie: Category A 50%, B 30%, C 20%, of a total of 600. How many units are in Category B?
hints: Multiply the percent by the total.

unsolved.problem: A slice spans 72°. What percent of the whole is it?
A budget pie has Savings at 15% of $4,000 monthly income. Annual savings?
A 25% slice equals 90 units. What is the grand total?
hints: 90 is a quarter of the total.

unsolved.problem: Pie X (total 2,000) shows Marketing at 10%. Pie Y (total 800) shows Marketing at 30%. Which has more Marketing staff?
hints: Convert each to a real count.

topics.name: Multi-Source Data Sets
topics.details: The hardest Data Interpretation sets give you two or more linked displays — say a table beside a bar graph, or a pie plus a line chart — and each question forces you to pull a number from one and a number from the other. The skill is cross-referencing: read what each display holds and how they connect (often a shared total or a shared category), then plan the two-step path before you calculate. A frequent structure gives totals in one figure and percentage breakdowns in another, so you multiply a percent from chart B by a total from chart A. Keep your units aligned across sources — one display might be in thousands and the other in raw counts. Because these questions chain operations, a small rounding slip early can push you to the wrong answer choice; when the choices are close, carry exact figures, and when they are far apart, estimate boldly and move on. Do not compute figures the question never asks for — multi-source displays deliberately include extra data as bait.

solved.problem: Chart A: total employees = 4,000. Chart B (a pie of employees): Engineering 25%, Sales 30%, Support 20%, Admin 25%. How many work in Sales?
Using the same charts, Chart C says 60% of Engineering staff hold a graduate degree. How many Engineering staff hold a graduate degree?
A table gives 2023 total revenue = $50M. A bar graph splits revenue by region: North 40%, South 35%, West 25%. How much more did North earn than West?

Quantitative Comparison. Chart A: City P has 20,000 households; City Q has 30,000. Chart B: 15% of P’s households and 8% of Q’s own an electric car. Quantity A: electric-car households in P. Quantity B: electric-car households in Q. Which is greater?
solved.solution: P: 0.15 × 20,000 = 3,000. Q: 0.08 × 30,000 = 2,400. 3,000 > 2,400, so Quantity A is greater. Both a percent (Chart B) and a total (Chart A) must be combined for each city.

unsolved.problem: Total students = 2,500 (Chart A). Chart B pie: Science 40%. How many study Science?
From the same set, Chart C says 30% of Science students take Physics. How many take Physics?
Table: total budget $8M. Bar chart: R&D is 45%. How much funds R&D?
City A has 10,000 homes, 12% with solar. City B has 8,000 homes, 20% with solar. Which city has more solar homes?
Chart A: 5,000 tickets sold. Chart B: 60% were adult tickets. Chart C: adult tickets cost $20 each. Total adult-ticket revenue?

shortcuts: Orient before you compute: read the title, axis labels, legend and units first — most DI errors are reading errors, not arithmetic.
Compute the grand total once, write it down, and reuse it across every linked question in the set.
If the answer choices are far apart, round hard and estimate — the on-screen basic calculator is slow; save it for close choices.
Convert a pie slice to a real value in one step: (slice percent) × grand total. Angle to percent: (angle/360) × 100.
On a line graph, the steepest segment is the greatest rate of change — you rarely need to read exact values to find it.
For "percent of total" always anchor to the grand total, never a row or column subtotal.
Never compare slices across two pies without first converting each to an absolute number using its own total.
mistakes: Ignoring "in thousands / millions" and reporting a raw table figure that is off by a factor of 1,000.
Taking a percent of the wrong whole — a category subtotal instead of the grand total.
Reading a truncated axis (starting above zero) as if bar differences were proportional to their heights.
Comparing pie slices across two charts by percent when the two totals differ.
Reading a stacked bar’s cumulative top as a single segment instead of subtracting the lower segment.
Computing extra values the question never asked for — multi-source sets bait you with irrelevant data.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — a pie shows Dept X at 20% of a 6,000-person firm; another firm’s Dept X is 30% of 3,000 people. Quantity A: heads in the first. Quantity B: heads in the second. Which is greater?
pyq.a: A = 0.20 × 6000 = 1200; B = 0.30 × 3000 = 900. Quantity A is greater. Convert percents to counts before comparing.

pyq.q: How are GRE Data Interpretation questions bundled?
pyq.a: In a set of 2–3 questions that all reference the same figure(s). Read the display thoroughly once; it pays back across every question.

pyq.q: A DI question gives choices of 12%, 20%, 33% and 50% for a percent increase from 250 to 300. How should you work?
pyq.a: The choices are far apart, so estimate: 50/250 = 1/5 = 20%. No calculator needed.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — a 25% pie slice equals 150 units. Enter the grand total.
pyq.a: 150 is one quarter of the total, so the total is 150 × 4 = 600.

flashcards.front: Greatest rate of change on a line graph
flashcards.back: the steepest segment (not the highest point)
convert each slice to an absolute number using its own total

flashcards.front: When to estimate vs use the calculator
flashcards.back: estimate when answer choices are far apart; calculate when close
subtract the segment below it from the cumulative top

summary: Data Interpretation bundles 2–3 questions on one figure; the maths is easy, the reading is where points are won or lost.
Always read the title, axis labels, legend and units before computing — and watch for "in thousands / millions".
Anchor every "percent of total" to the grand total, and compute that total once to reuse across the set.
Turn a pie slice into a value with (slice percent) × grand total; convert angles via (angle/360) × 100.
On line graphs the slope is the story: the steepest segment marks the fastest change.
Never compare slices across two pies by percent alone — convert each to an absolute count first.
Estimate boldly when answer choices are far apart; reserve the slow on-screen calculator for close calls.
